title: The prayer at the river
hook: ten kings against one, at a river. the Rig Veda remembers the battle by a family's prayer, and how they always end it
carry: svasti: ask all the gods to keep us well

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashvins in the Rig Veda, the twin healers. The Ashvins: healing is holy work.

Ten kings, joined against one. In the Rig Veda's seventh book, King Sudas faces an alliance of ten, near a river called the Parushni. His priest is the sage Vasishtha. The odds are terrible. And what the hymns remember isn't a battle plan. It's a prayer. Vasishtha's family called on Indra, the hymns say, and Indra heard them. Today, the last day on these four voices: what Vasishtha's family asks for at the end, every time.
screen: `TEN KINGS AGAINST ONE.` → `NOT A BATTLE PLAN. A PRAYER.` → `HOW THE HYMNS END.`

segments.voice: The battle of the ten kings is one of the few events in the Rig Veda that reads like history, and it's remembered in the hymns of Vasishtha's family. In paraphrase, from book seven: like thirsting men, surrounded in the battle of the ten kings, they looked up to the sky, and Indra heard Vasishtha as he praised him. Another hymn gives the victory to Indra and Varuna together: the ten kings could not overcome Sudas. Now listen to how so many of this family's hymns end. Not with a boast. With one line, the same line, hymn after hymn: yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. You all, protect us always with blessings. Yuyam is you, plural: all of you, every god at once. Svasti is well-being, things going well. After praise of Indra, after a plea to Varuna, after a song to the dawn, the sign-off doesn't change. Here's the teaching. Asking the gods for svasti, well-being, is one of the oldest prayers Hindus have, and it's still said. Another Rig Veda verse, chanted today as a peace prayer before study and worship, is a string of them: svasti na indro, may Indra give us well-being; may Pushan, may the great bird Tarkshya, may Brihaspati. When you don't know which god to ask, the hymns' answer is simple: ask them all, and ask for well-being.
screen: `TEN KINGS. INDRA HEARD VASISHTHA.` · `YUYAM PATA SVASTIBHIH SADA NAH.` · `YUYAM: ALL OF YOU.` · `SVASTI NA INDRO: STILL CHANTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you'll see or worry about today, one face at a time. If you pray, say svasti for each, may it go well, then widen it the way yuyam does, to all of them at once and everyone they love. If you don't, wish each face one plain thing: be well. End the way the hymns end, the same way every time: keep us well, always.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, how so many of the Vasishtha family's hymns close: you all, protect us always with well-being. Today's word.
Your line: svasti, ask all the gods to keep us well. Yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. Four voices, heard.

notes: Refrain yūyaṃ pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ: confirm it closes hymns in Rig Veda book 7 to Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna (e.g. 7.1, 7.20, 7.77, 7.86); 'hymn after hymn' is used instead of a count.
Confirm that Rig Veda 7.86 (the Varuna hymn of day 1271, written by another writer) ends with this refrain; if not, cut the sentence linking the two.
Glosses: yūyam 'you (plural)', pāta 'protect', svastibhiḥ 'with blessings / well-being', sadā 'always', naḥ 'us'; confirm.
'Not victory, not riches, though other verses ask for those' is a general statement about Vedic requests; confirm or trim.
Svasti glossed without etymology on purpose. Devanagari स्वस्ति; confirm.
